column1: In software architecture, what makes a Module “deep”?
column2: A deep Module provides a lot of useful behavior behind a small Interface that callers do not need to understand in detail.

column1: When evaluating a possible refactor, what does the deletion test ask?
column2: If the Module were deleted, would its complexity disappear or reappear across multiple callers?
Related behavior, bugs, and change knowledge are concentrated in one Module instead of spread across callers.
Callers get more capability from less Interface knowledge because one Implementation pays off across many call sites and tests.

column1: What does “the Interface is the test surface” mean?
column2: Tests should verify behavior through the same Interface callers use, rather than reaching into scattered Implementation details.

column1: What question helps detect when a caller is helping implement a Module instead of using it?
column2: Is the caller making implementation decisions such as mapping types, checking invariants, validating paths, or special-casing variants?

column1: Why does a deeper Module not eliminate complexity?
column2: It moves real complexity behind the right Interface so callers do not all have to participate in it.

column1: How are architectural seams and Module seams related?
column2: Architectural seams separate large layers like routes and workflows, while Module seams apply the same idea at a smaller scale inside those layers.
